design_detail: Secondary analysis of the Cochrane living systematic review of electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation (data to January 2022), with protocol registered in advance (OSF). It regroups participants of nine studies by what they actually did after being given an e-cigarette (e-cigarette only, cigarettes only, both, neither) rather than by assigned arm, and compares biomarkers of potential harm: exhaled carbon monoxide (pooled by inverse-variance random-effects meta-analysis where at least two studies allowed) and 25 other biomarkers (effect direction plots, because most were reported by single studies). Only one low-risk-of-bias study is among the nine and it contributes no pooled estimate.
can_establish: How biomarkers of exposure to combustion products compared, in nine short-term studies in which adults who smoked were given e-cigarettes, between groups defined by their later behaviour (e-cigarette only, cigarettes only, both, neither), with the direction and, for exhaled carbon monoxide, the size of the differences.
cannot_establish: That switching caused the lower values (the groups were formed by behaviour, not randomized, and 8 of 9 studies were at high risk of bias), that the differences last or lead to less disease (follow-up 1 week to 8 months, no clinical outcome), how much nicotine people took in (not analysed), or what happens outside trials and confinement units.

sample.recruitment: Studies of e-cigarette interventions given to adults who smoke, for smoking cessation (randomized trials, cross-over trials and non-randomized intervention studies), found in the Cochrane living review searches; countries Greece, Italy, Poland, the United Kingdom and the United States. Baseline participants per study (Table 2): Cobb 520, Cravo 419, Goniewicz 22, Ikonomidis 90, Kerr 55, McRobbie 40, Morris 79, Pacifici 34, Pulvers 40 (sum 1299).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Studies had to report exhaled carbon monoxide or any other known biomarker of potential harm at 1 week or longer from study start, with data available by observed or self-reported use of e-cigarettes and cigarettes. Where several time points existed, the longest follow-up was used.
sample.demographics: Not reported in this paper (see the parent Cochrane review).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; participant numbers in each regrouped comparison are not reported in the text (forest plots are images).
sample.selection_effects: Only 7 of the 49 parent-review studies with biomarker data reported them by actual product use, plus two newer studies. Behaviour-defined groups are self-selected after randomization (people who switched completely may differ from those who kept smoking). Two studies were confined units for 1 to 2 weeks. The abstainer comparison rests on one University of Glasgow document that appears to be a thesis (Kerr 2020: 12 abstainers, 16 in the e-cigarette group, 3 smoking).

exposure.measurement: Observed or self-reported use of e-cigarettes and cigarettes during each study, as extracted from the original reports; groups: e-cigarette only, cigarette only, both, neither.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as recorded, not recommendations. Device types by Table 2: cig-a-like (3 studies), refillable (3), pod (1), cartridge (1), not clear (1). Follow-up 1 week to 8 months (Cravo 1 week; Goniewicz 1 and 2 weeks; Morris 2 weeks; McRobbie and Pulvers 4 weeks; Ikonomidis 1 month; Kerr 12 weeks; Cobb 3 months; Pacifici 1, 4 and 8 months). In one study with 8-month values (the only one in Table 2 with that time point is Pacifici 2015) the cigarette group cut from 27 to 8 cigarettes per day and the dual group from 23 to 5 (Figure 1 and 2 legends). Nicotine content, flavours and puffing patterns are not analysed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (exhaled carbon monoxide and urinary or blood markers at the study's follow-up point).

comparison.controls: Within each study, participants who smoked cigarettes only, who used an e-cigarette and cigarettes (dual use), or who used neither (abstainers; one study).
comparison.matching: None; unadjusted comparisons of behaviour groups (mostly absolute values at follow-up, some change from baseline).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Whatever drives who switches completely versus who keeps smoking (dependence, motivation, health); the authors note unmeasured confounding in the non-randomized groupings.

outcomes.instruments: Exhaled carbon monoxide (parts per million) and one blood carbon monoxide measure (carboxyhaemoglobin saturation); 25 urinary biomarker rows in Table 1 (mercapturic acids, the nitrosamine metabolite NNAL, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites and other carcinogen metabolites); the abstract says 26.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors call these 'biomarkers of potential harm'; they measure exposure to combustion products and carcinogens, not disease. They deliberately did not analyse nicotine exposure, which they say is not necessarily a measure of harm.
outcomes.operationalization: Lower biomarker value = less exposure. For markers other than carbon monoxide, 'lower' is judged from an effect direction plot: two arrows when the 95% intervals or error bars did not overlap, one arrow when no interval or P value was given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; no formal test of 25 biomarkers.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled exhaled CO (inverse-variance random effects, RevMan 5): e-cigarette versus cigarettes, mean difference -9.57 ppm (95% CI -17.30 to -1.83), 3 studies; e-cigarette versus both, -4.40 ppm (-12.04 to 3.24), 2 studies; both versus cigarettes only, -1.91 ppm (-3.38 to -0.45), 2 studies. I-squared substantial in all, which the authors say reflects size rather than direction of effect (forest plots are images; abstract values used). Other biomarkers (Table 1): 12 of 13 lower with e-cigarette than cigarettes, 1 not different (NNN); e-cigarette versus both: 12 of 25 lower with e-cigarette, 5 lower with both, 8 unclear or inconsistent; both versus cigarettes only (one study): 12 of 13 lower with both, NNN not different.
analysis.covariates: None (unadjusted group comparisons); one included trial (Cobb 2021) used covariates in mixed models, reported without data.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Protocol registered in advance on OSF (https://osf.io/g6bw3/); deviations are not mentioned; the protocol was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Effect direction plots replace pooling for 25 biomarkers; the text notes Study 1 of Morris was shown because it was larger, and that Pulvers' two small groups (n = 6 and n = 21) were the ones compared.
analysis.power: Pooled analyses combine only 2 to 3 studies each; for carbon monoxide the baseline levels were low in all groups (figure legends).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In nine short-term studies (1 week to 8 months; 8 at high risk of bias; 2 industry-funded), exhaled carbon monoxide was lower in people who used only e-cigarettes than in people who kept smoking (by about 10 ppm in three studies, interval 1.8 to 17.3) and by a smaller amount in people who used both than in people who only smoked (about 2 ppm in two studies, 0.5 to 3.4). It was not clearly different between people who used only e-cigarettes and people who used both (interval -12.0 to 3.2). For other biomarkers, 12 of 13 were lower with e-cigarettes than with cigarettes, mostly from two industry-funded studies; against dual use, 12 of 25 were lower with e-cigarettes and 5 (all polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites, from a single 22-person study with no intervals) were higher.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that switching from smoking to vaping or dual use 'appears to reduce levels of biomarkers of potential harm significantly'. The Discussion adds that the studies showed no evidence that biomarkers rose in people who kept smoking while also using e-cigarettes, and that the findings fit other observational studies.

timeline.event: Goniewicz et al.: PATH cross-sectional comparison of urinary biomarkers in people who only vaped, only smoked, both, or neither (card sc_goniewicz_2018).

Akiyama and Sherwood systematic review of biomarker findings from nine clinical studies of e-cigarettes and heated tobacco products, cited by the authors as finding lower toxicant levels in people using e-cigarettes than cigarettes (not read here).
Parent Cochrane living review of e-cigarettes for smoking cessation (Hartmann-Boyce et al.), from which this analysis is drawn (not read here).

replication.where_it_stands: The direction (lower exhaled carbon monoxide and combustion-product markers with exclusive e-cigarette use than with continued smoking) is consistent across the studies pooled here and with the PATH comparison, but rests on short follow-up and mostly high-risk-of-bias studies. The reassurance about dual use rests on few studies; the 2023 paper itself calls for individual participant data and longer studies.

funding.funder: Oxford University Public Policy Challenge Grant; Cancer Research UK Tobacco Advisory Group Project Grant; core infrastructure funding from the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) for the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Review Group. No tobacco or e-cigarette industry funding is declared for the review.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: five authors declare none. Hajek provided consultancy to and received research funding from Pfizer. Bullen is an investigator on grants from the Health Research Council of New Zealand, the Australian NHMRC, the NZ Ministry of Health and Auckland Council, and has provided consultancy to J&J Japan on nicotine-replacement products. Rigotti has received royalties from UpToDate for chapters on electronic cigarettes and, outside e-cigarettes, has consulted for and received a research grant from Achieve Life Sciences.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors are at the University of Oxford (Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences; Department for Continuing Education), Queen Mary University of London (Wolfson Institute of Population Health), the University of Auckland, and Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School. Two of the nine included studies (Cravo 2016, Morris 2022) are marked in Table 2 as tobacco or e-cigarette industry funded; no other funder of the included studies is named.

what_would_settle_it: Individual participant data from the trials, with biomarkers measured at several time points in people who switched completely, kept smoking, or did both, adjusted for baseline smoking, with device and nicotine content recorded, follow-up of at least a year, and clinical outcomes measured in the same people.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Adults who smoke given e-cigarettes; four behaviour-defined groups; carbon monoxide and listed biomarkers; follow-up of at least 1 week.
Protocol registered in advance on OSF and the parent Cochrane protocol exists; the registered plan was not read and deviations are not mentioned.
Randomized, cross-over and non-randomized intervention studies are included 'as per the parent review'; no reason is given here for mixing designs when regrouping by behaviour.

Seven sources (Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP); strategy and restrictions are in the parent review (not read); reference 5 (Kerr 2020) is a University of Glasgow document that appears to be a thesis; no reference-list searching is described here.
Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts; disagreements resolved by discussion or a third reviewer.
Study characteristics and risk of bias in duplicate in the parent review; for this analysis one reviewer extracted outcome data and a second checked it.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The main text gives no list of the 42 biomarker studies not used; the flow diagram is in the supporting information (not read) and a list may be in the parent review.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 2 gives device type, baseline N, groups, outcomes and time points, data type, risk of bias, industry funding and country; population, nicotine content and use patterns are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane methods in duplicate in the parent review, one overall judgment per study (8 high, 1 low); the tool is not named here and the judgments concern the original comparisons, not the behaviour-defined regrouping.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Table 2 flags tobacco or e-cigarette industry funding yes or no for each study (two yes); other funders are not named.

Inverse-variance random effects, with heterogeneity noted and pooling justified by consistent direction; but groups formed by post-randomization behaviour are combined as raw values or changes without adjustment, with 2 to 3 studies per estimate.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No sensitivity or subgroup analysis by risk of bias; 8 of 9 studies are rated high.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion states that the data come from short confinement studies or from non-randomized groupings open to unmeasured confounding; the 'high' ratings in Table 2 are not discussed in the text.
Substantial I-squared for exhaled carbon monoxide, said to reflect size rather than direction of effect.
Not tested because no pooled analysis had 10 studies; the parent review found no evidence of publication bias but could not rule it out.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Interests of each author and the review's funders are printed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can be judged only from the supporting information and the parent review, which were not read. On the items that can be judged, two critical items are 'no' (11: unadjusted pooling of behaviour-defined groups; 15: no publication-bias assessment, for a reason the authors give) and three are only partly met (2, 4, 9), which mechanically gives critically low confidence. This is a judgment about how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not about the authors' candour: they state the confinement and non-randomized-grouping limits and say what is missing (individual participant data, longer studies). The paper may be cited for the direction of the biomarker differences and for the pooled exhaled-carbon-monoxide differences as short-term, high-risk-of-bias findings; not for the size of any benefit of switching, for dual use being protective, or for any health outcome.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC10092879 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2, figure legends, declaration of interests, acknowledgements, references; Figures 1 to 3 are forest plots rendered as images and their values were not extracted, the pooled values are those printed in the abstract; Supporting information (flow diagram) not read; the parent Cochrane review not read)

key_findings.finding: Nine studies (1299 adults who smoked and were given e-cigarettes) were included: seven of 49 parent-review studies with biomarker data, plus two newer ones (Kerr 2020, Morris 2022). Settings: Greece, Italy, Poland, UK, US.

Overall risk of bias was high in 8 of 9 studies and low in 1 (Cobb 2021, 520 participants); two studies are marked as tobacco or e-cigarette industry funded (Cravo 2016, n = 419; Morris 2022, n = 79). Follow-up 1 week to 8 months; devices were cig-a-like, refillable, pod, cartridge or unclear.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, columns 'Overall risk of bias judgement', 'Tobacco or EC industry funding?', 'Outcomes available (time-point)', 'Device type'

key_findings.finding: Pooled exhaled carbon monoxide (ppm): e-cigarette only versus cigarettes only, mean difference -9.57 (95% CI -17.30 to -1.83), 3 studies; e-cigarette only versus both, -4.40 (-12.04 to 3.24), 2 studies; both versus cigarettes only, -1.91 (-3.38 to -0.45), 2 studies. Heterogeneity substantial in every comparison, said to reflect magnitude, not direction.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Findings; Results › Carbon monoxide, 1st paragraph; Figures 1 to 3 (images, values not extracted)
key_findings.note: Forest plots were images; the pooled values are those in the abstract.

key_findings.finding: Figure legends: baseline exhaled carbon monoxide was low in all groups; in one study with 8-month values the cigarette-only group cut from 27 to 8 cigarettes per day and the dual-use group from 23 to 5 (Table 2 suggests Pacifici 2015).

The only data on abstainers (Kerr 2020, reference 5, a University of Glasgow document that appears to be a thesis): exhaled carbon monoxide at 12 weeks was 1 ppm (SD 1) in both the e-cigarette group (n = 16) and abstainers (n = 12); abstainers were 18.00 ppm lower than the cigarette group (n = 3; 95% CI -24.81 to -11.19).

Blood carbon monoxide (carboxyhaemoglobin saturation) at day 14 in the confinement study of Morris et al. (study 1): e-cigarette versus cigarettes mean difference -7.13 (95% CI -8.41 to -5.85); e-cigarette versus both -2.56 (-3.81 to -1.31); both versus cigarettes -4.57 (-5.90 to -3.25). Participants used e-cigarettes only for days 1 to 9, then were randomized to e-cigarette, cigarettes or both for days 10 to 14.
key_findings.locator: Results › Carbon monoxide, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 footnote

key_findings.finding: Other biomarkers came from five studies (none on abstainers). Cigarette-only comparison (13 biomarkers): 12 lower with e-cigarettes, none higher, one (NNN) not different; Table 1 shows these rows rest on Cravo 2016 and Morris 2022 only, both industry-funded and rated high risk of bias.
key_findings.locator: Results › Other biomarkers, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, column 'EC versus CC'; Table 2

key_findings.finding: E-cigarette-only versus dual use (25 biomarkers): 12 lower with e-cigarettes, 5 lower with dual use (all five are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites, single-arrow entries from Goniewicz 2017, n = 22), 8 not different or inconsistent. Dual use versus cigarettes only (one study, Morris 2022; 13 biomarkers): 12 lower with dual use, NNN not different.
key_findings.locator: Results › Other biomarkers, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, columns 'EC versus EC + CC' and 'Dual use (EC + CC) versus CC'
key_findings.note: Three of the 12 'lower with e-cigarettes' rows (MHBMA, 3-hydroxyfluorene, 2-naphthol) carry single arrows (point estimates, no interval or P value).

key_findings.finding: In McRobbie 2015 a mercapturic acid marker (named '3-HMPA' in the text; see reporting issues) fell significantly in both the e-cigarette-only and dual-use groups over 4 weeks, with no between-group difference in the change (mean difference 194.00 ng/g, 95% CI -502 to 890); the authors say this was the only biomarker other than carbon monoxide with data that could have been meta-analysed.

Authors' limits: data come from short confinement studies not readily generalizable, or from non-randomized groupings open to unmeasured confounding; for all outcomes but carbon monoxide data were very limited and precluded meta-analysis; products varied; no individual participant data; nicotine exposure not analysed; only one study gave data on abstainers.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results sentence on the single study comparing dual use with cigarettes says 12 of 13 biomarkers 'were lower in EC'; the abstract and Table 1 show they were lower in the dual-use group.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Other biomarkers, 2nd paragraph; Abstract › Findings
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence should read 'dual use'; cite the abstract's wording.

reporting_issues.issue: The text names the McRobbie biomarker '3-hydroxy-1-methylpropyl-mercapturic acid (3-HMPA)', but Table 1 files McRobbie under 3-HPMA (3-hydroxypropylmercapturic acid), a different compound.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which compound the McRobbie result refers to; the study title names acrolein, which fits 3-HPMA.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 12 biomarkers were lower for e-cigarette than dual use and the Results add '(95% CI/error bars non-overlapping)', but three of the 12 rows in Table 1 carry single arrows, which the Table 1 key defines as having no interval, error bar or P value.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Other biomarkers, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 key
reporting_issues.consequence: 'Significantly lower' in the abstract overstates the evidence for those three rows; at most 9 rows have a stated interval or error bar.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 lists exhaled carbon monoxide among Morris 2022's outcomes, but the Results report blood carboxyhaemoglobin for that study, not breath carbon monoxide.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which studies feed the pooled exhaled carbon monoxide estimates cannot be confirmed from the text; Figure 1 footnotes suggest the three studies are Ikonomidis 2018, Kerr 2020 and Pacifici 2015, but the forest plots are images.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract refers to 26 other biomarkers; Table 1 has 25 rows (26 only if the combined '3-, 4-hydroxyphenanthrenes' row counts as two). Table 1 also contains typographical slips ('Morris%60' in the 3-HMPMA row; 'Gonieciwz' in the footnote).
reporting_issues.consequence: Immaterial to conclusions; cite '25 biomarker rows in Table 1'.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say four exhaled carbon monoxide studies could be pooled, while the abstract gives pooled analyses of 3, 2 and 2 studies and the Figure 2 legend has three footnoted entries.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Carbon monoxide, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Findings; Figure 2 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: The study count behind the e-cigarette-versus-both estimate (2 in the abstract) cannot be confirmed without the forest plot.
